utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, there is somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor who was attempting to come into court somehow in the public gallery, if you could call it a public gallery in this funny little shoe box. The Rule is that when we have a protected witness, as we have now, nobody is permitted into the public gallery because there is no way in which we can have screens put around the witness because the interpreters are all cut off. Now, if you want to have somebody that you can identify as a person from the OTP sitting in there, that's perfectly all right, but it has to be made as an application and have it recorded in the transcript, I'm afraid. Do you know who we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about an intern who actually has a make to summary of this witness's testimony but she can do it also in our rooms with the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it's a matter for you. I would certainly say that she could do so in those circumstances because it's rather like the one we had in the other courtroom the other day during the closed court, but you can understand that this tiny little room over there that they call the public gallery has full view of the witness, so it is shut and nobody is entitled to go in there without permission, you see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the fact that this courtroom is very small and we have not much space here, I rather think she should do it in our rooms and just watch the proceedings on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. If that's all right from your point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, this new witness, FWS-69.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before you go on, I'm afraid that we are caught, we are going to be in this courtroom for a week or so. It's because the other two trials have multiple accused and neither of them can come into this tiny little room. I'm sorry about that, but we have indeed been discriminated against. I don't think there's any Article in the statute that would permit us to charge the registrar, but nevertheless, we are being discriminated against. Yes, now, sir, will you please take the solemn declaration that you are being shown by the court usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Will you please sit down, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The pseudonym document will be Exhibit P439, and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in front of you you have a sheet of paper with the witness number 69 on it, and below this number there is a name. Is it your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And below your name there is a date. Is it your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Underneath your date of birth there is a reference to a profession. Is it your profession and your working place from before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Underneath your profession there is a name. Is it the name of your cousin who was later detained at KP Dom together with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Below this name there is another name. Is it the name of your uncle?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Whenever you want to refer to these persons during your testimony, do not call them by their names because that would reveal your identity. Simply call them "uncle" or "cousin." Below, you will find some more names of protected persons, and when you want to refer to these persons, do not use their names, just use their pseudonym, their number, or their initials. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Jelec, the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: By ethnicity, I'm a Bosniak, a Muslim, and my religion is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you have children? Are you married and do you have children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, I am, and I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where did you live in Foca, in which neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I live in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Foca in April 1992, where were you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: In April 1992, in fact, before April 1992, I don't know the exact date but I know it was Bajram, I went with my children and my family to the village of Jelec.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And where is Jelec situated in relation to Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Its a 20 kilometres away from Foca, along the road to Miljevina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is it a Muslim settlement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it's 95 to 98 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many people lived in Foca at that time? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: In Foca --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the village, and we are talking about Jelec.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: As far as I remember, according to the census of 1990 or 1995 and the electoral lists, there were about 890 or so members with voting rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what would that mean? Do you know how many people lived there altogether, including the children? Approximately. Not the exact number, of course.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: If there were 890 to 900, according to the census, that must mean that a half of this number were other members, other family members.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how many houses belonged to Jelec? Approximately, not the exact number of, of course.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I don't know precisely, but it can be 400 to 450 houses, including surrounding hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was the last time that you went to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: The last time I went to work was Monday, in the month of April. I was to report to work then, but I didn't go then. I went on Tuesday, and it was the 1st or the 2nd of April, the day after Bajram.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why did you stop to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I came to work that day - it was the Tuesday after Bajram. It must have been the second or the third day of Bajram. When I arrived at work in the school centre outside Aladza, there were very few pupils outside the school. When I came inside, I asked why there were no students, and the director told me that they hadn't come. I asked what we were supposed to do, and they said, "Wait. Wait for the students to come." I waited for a while, for a couple of hours, and then the director said we should go home. I asked, "What are we going to do tomorrow?" He said, "Report to work." So I went home, and when I came home, a friend of mine who worked at the hospital called me around 1.00 p.m. and told me to get ready quickly and come to fetch her in order for us to go together to my village in Jelec. I picked her up from the hospital. We came back home. She told me that the situation wasn't good, that she had been told by a colleague of hers, her friend with whom she worked by the name of Milojka. This woman told her, "Take your children and get away from Foca quickly." So my wife and I came back home. There were barricades around, roadblocks around the town. We picked up the minimum of things we could and we went to my village, to Jelec, and we arrived there without encountering any problems or roadblocks. That's how I came to Jelec. We spent the night there, but I was supposed to report to work again the next day and she was too. From my home, the town centre was about a kilometre away or perhaps 800 metres, and when we came to the centre, buses were leaving, taking workers to Maglic, to Foca, but the buses hadn't arrived. Many citizens were there waiting for the buses. I wanted to continue in my own car, but I was told I could not. They told me that beginning with Miljevina, there were roadblocks on the roads. A man coming from Miljevina said that we couldn't go there, that that night, in his warehouses and on the premises of Maglic, army troops had arrived, raided the premises. They were commanded by a man called Zeka. They told the employees to go home and that the premises were taken over by the Serbian army. And they installed a roadblock, in fact, they put a bulldozer on the road, across the road. So he arrived to Jelec frightened --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you. We would not need all the details of what happened here and there. Just answer my questions and do not give us all these details. What I would like to know from you is why did you go to Jelec? Did you feel safer there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I shall reply to that question based on my experience from the Second World War, Foca was an unstable place, unsafe. I know the history very well, and I know the stories from the war. In Foca, I don't know which year in the Second World War, Foca saw a genocide, a massacre of the Muslim population. Two or 3.000 people were killed in one day on the bridge on the Drina. Based on the same experience, no one in my village got killed in the same war. The neighbours were good, tolerant, friendly, and that's why I felt safe there. That's why I decided to be in Jelec.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you own a house in Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I had an old house, inherited from my father, my parents, and together with my brother, I built another big house. I had finished it that year. So I stayed in my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said already that you and your wife and your children went to Jelec and that you actually wanted to go to work from there and you were stopped at the barricade. This barricade, who operated it? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I personally never reached the roadblocks. The roadblocks were about a kilometre away, and it was at the exit from Miljevina in the village of Rataja, and at the roadblock, according to these stories from this Haso Suljevic, it was manned from locals from Miljevina, Serbian soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms. They were manning the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Jelec following this block?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: We stayed in Jelec until the 4th of May, when I was captured and transferred to the camp of the KP Dom in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Muslims in Jelec continue to live their normal life or did they organise themselves to protect themselves?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Afterwards in Jelec - that was on the 6th or the 7th of April - we were listening to the news. We had telephone connection was Miljevina, we had telephone contacts and we listened to the radio. It was quiet in Jelec. Combat had started already in Foca on the 7th or the 8th of April. I don't know exactly. The news we heard was that fighting was going on, that the health centre had been captured, that there was fighting in Aladza and that the situation was difficult in Foca. We could hear the sound of shelling from mortars and other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you, you the residents in Jelec, what did you do to protect yourselves?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Jelec were confused and frightened. We watched tanks going towards Miljevina from Kalinovik through Mladi Gaj, in Budanj, earth was being bulldozed in order to install cannons and other weapons, and the situation was generally difficult. We could hear shooting. We can see Budanj from Jelec and other villages beyond Budanj. We could see houses burning, we could see the smoke rising high, and hear the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you set up guard posts? I mean not you personally but the villagers in Jelec.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, we did. The inhabitants of Foca -- of Jelec did, because I was from Foca and I spent only the weekends in Jelec. I spent most of my time in Foca. Those sentry posts were at the entrance to Jelec, below a place called Stavanj, the former railway station. That's where some sentry posts were. Others were below Gradina towards Miljevina, and another sentry post, third one, was even closer to Jelec. There was a primary school there where I was summoned one day, because my house is 800 metres away from the centre, and I was told, "You have been summoned to stand guard here." I had no weapons. There were people from the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA of Jelec. There was Ibro, Tano, Sljivo --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we do not need all the details. Please wait for my questions and answer the questions. What were the persons on the guard posts supposed to do? Why did they stand guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: When I was summoned and told that I am to stand guard, they told me that my assignment was to stand guard for two hours, and my duty was if somebody came from the direction of Miljevina or if I see a personnel carrier, to fire one shot to warn the population of Jelec that they should flee their houses, and they were ready to withdraw to nearby woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did the villagers and what did you fear what would happen if soldiers came into Jelec? Why did you organise this kind of alarm?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Well, people were afraid. Everybody was afraid for their lives, the lives of their children. They were experiencing normal fear. We could also hear the news of what was going on in Sarajevo and in other places. Electricity was cut off, the radio wasn't working, but we could hear news on small battery-fed radios. We could hear on the news that houses were burning, that people were being killed, and of course people were frightened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said you were summoned once. Did you actually then stand guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: When I was summoned, I was told that I was to stand guard for two hours. They told me it was my obligation, and I agreed. I had no weapon, although I did have a pistol and a licence for it, but they told me I didn't need a gun. They told me, "You'll receive a rifle when you get there."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How often did you stand guard in this kind of manner, only once or several times?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this period, did you actually observe burning villages, other villages burning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, we could see that. Not Jelec, but only the villages beyond Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Miljevina, Danicici, Hrmalusa, Kozja, Luka, Budanj, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are these Muslim villages? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I don't know precisely because I wasn't there, but we supposed those were the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Serbs and the Muslims in Jelec negotiate at some point in time, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, they did negotiate. Delegations came from Miljevina two or three times. I wasn't present and I couldn't hear what the negotiations were about because the negotiations were with the people from Jelec who were permanent residents, but I only heard what other people said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know who the people were that came from Miljevina to negotiate? Do you know -- not the names. Do you know their positions? Were they soldiers or were they connected to whatever authority?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Can I mention their names?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If you know them, yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I cannot say chronologically who came the first time, who the second time or the third time, but I know that once the delegation from Miljevina included Colonel Stankovic, Mr. Elez, Cico Gojko, Cedo Zelovic, and I don't remember the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said Colonel Stankovic, a Colonel from where? Do you know where he came from? Was he a JNA officer or what?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely. I know he was born in Miljevina. I don't know whether he was a reserve Colonel or an active-duty colonel, but I think in all probability he was a reserve, a Colonel in reserve forces, or perhaps he was retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What were the Muslims -- you said you were not present during the negotiation. Did you, nevertheless, learn what the Muslims were requested to do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: From the Muslims who had been there and from what they told me, I know that they had insisted that we surrender the weapons we had, that we do not fight, do not make war. They wanted peace to continue, the sowing season to go on, and that's the first version of negotiations. The second time when they came, an ultimatum was set, together with a deadline for surrendering hunting and other weapons. All weapons were to be surrendered in order for peace to be maintained.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what was the deadline? Do you know what date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: People were given one day to surrender weapons and the deadline was a Friday. I think it was the 28th or the 29th of April or perhaps the 1st of May. The weapons were to be surrendered until noon. My neighbours told me, "You have a pistol. Prepare your pistol and all the ammunition you have and come before noon to turn it in."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Muslims in Jelec ever call the JNA for help? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I found out about that. I was not present there, but I found out from other people that sometime around the 25th of April or the 20th of April, I don't know exactly, in Jelec, within this delegation from Miljevina, there was Colonel Pavlovic from Miljevina. When they talked, the people of Jelec lived in fear. There was an ultimatum to surrender their weapons. Dzemal Hadzic from Jelec wanted the arms to be surrendered, but Colonel Pavlovic should send 20 to 25 to 30 soldiers to be stationed in Jelec, I don't know the exact number, and that they would be provided with ample food and that in Jelec they should have the Yugoslav army. Pavlovic did not meet that request he said that that was not within his domain, and that he would not do that and then he said if anything bothered you, if anything was difficult for you, escape to Kalinovik. Kalinovik is Turkey for you. You should feel very safe up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And this Colonel Pavlovic, was he from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: He was an active officer in Kalinovik. From the JNA. Yes, from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When this ultimatum was issued, what did the villagers of Jelec decide to do? Did you intend to hand over your weapons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: The ultimatum was on that Friday that I mentioned, at 12.00. Before that Friday, people were told to come to Jelec, everybody, all the locals. That was the afternoon or, rather, sometime in the evening hours to the former carpet factory, the big hall there. I came to this meeting. I wanted to tell them something at that meeting. I was present there, but there were people also in the street and on the road. Must have been 150 men. There were men mostly but there were some women as well. At these -- at this meeting, many people took part in the discussion, and they were wondering whether they would hand over their weapons, whether they would not hand over their weapons, and it was decided that on the next day, weapons should be handed over for the sake of peace, for the sake of stability. Jelec did not have any weapons, Jelec did not have any army. Jelec decided to hand over its weapons in order to leave in peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually hand over the weapons the following day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: The next day, Friday, I had been sleeping at my house. When I got up, it might have been around 7.00 in the morning, I don't know exactly, there were people in front of my house, people who went to town and were coming back. They said, "Guess what's up?" That day we were supposed to hand in our weapons at 12.00, and they told me that some kind of military had arrived in Jelec. So with them, I returned to town again to see what was going on over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of army had arrived in Jelec, or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I came to the restaurant down in the centre of town. There weren't any. There were lots of locals from Jelec. I did not see them. I said, "Where are they"? And they said, "They are over there in the carpet factory." In the meantime, I got they got there from the carpet factory. I saw two or three soldiers in uniform. They had camouflage uniforms. It was the first time that I had seen insignia of that kind. There were two or three soldiers in uniform and six or seven soldiers who were carrying hunting weapons, rifles. He Did not introduce himself to me, but they told me that that was Major Besovic who had arrived, I don't know where from. At that moment, some people asked him, "What are you doing here? Are you guaranteeing security to these people here? What is going to happen to all these people?" He replied -- I mean, they were getting into the restaurant and they wanted to sit in the restaurant. And he said, "Who's going to guarantee my security? Everybody guarantees his own security." Again when people insisted, saying that there were so many women and children there, that all of this population was unprotected, and he said everybody guarantees his own security. He came -- he said, "I'm not here to protect Jelec. I am protecting Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these soldiers that had arrived, were they Muslims or what were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I don't know their names and surnames. I found out there were people there from Visegrad. It was as if Visegrad had been occupied and that they got out of Visegrad, having taken some weapons. Besovic was there. They told me that that was him, but he hadn't introduced himself. I don't know about the others; Muslims most probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the villagers of Jelec join the Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: In terms of who guaranteed whose security, his answer was, "I'm not asking you to join us. We're not forcing you to do that. It's a matter of everyone's own free will. Who wants to join us may but who doesn't want to doesn't have to." That was his answer, and some people from Jelec did join him. I don't know who they are. And he left. He got going. As they were leaving our people, they passed by the former barracks. They crossed the bridge, and they came to the hill of Stavanj. With him were perhaps about ten people, and then they were joined perhaps by a few locals from Jelec. I don't know exactly how many. He said that he also had another platoon of some ten men and that they were going up to Gradina. So they left, and I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How far is this hill that you just mentioned away from the residential areas of Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Well, as the crow flies, perhaps about one kilometre. I don't know whether this is very accurate, but there is nearby. This is a hill above Jelec which you can see very well. It is basically right above Jelec. You can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was Jelec attacked on that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: On that day when I arrived home, people were upset. People were terrified. When I got home, together with my neighbours, we decided to leave our homes, to flee from our homes. We decided to flee to the forest below the mountain of Husac. So we left with our children, our wives. In the meantime, from the village of Jelec, we saw people fleeing to the hills even before we had left. I left my house on the 1st of May. It was a sunny day. We took some things, as many as we could carry in our hands. We went uphill. We were walking through the woods and along the meadows. When we got about one kilometre away from my house, the first shells already started hitting Jelec from the direction of Miljevina. As we continued our journey, 200 or 300 metres later then we heard sounds from the direction of Kalinovik. We thought that these were jet planes. After that, very loud explosions were heard in Jelec. The earth was shaking. We were really scared. We tried to run away as far as we could from Jelec, as far as into the forest as we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many villagers were fleeing with you? Can you give us a proximate number?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: The village of Jelec is a centre -- I don't know how they were actually running away. However, they all got out of Jelec. On the other hand, the right bank of the river, you could see people escaping there from Sokolina, Cilec [phoen], Vis. People were leaving their houses and running into the forest. I could notice that. As for Jelec specifically, I don't know exactly. It depended on how fast people could move. There were grandmothers, grandfathers, children. So it was the entire population of the village running away. It was an exodus, so you can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did residents remain in Jelec? Did people remain in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I forgot to tell you something. In the meantime, from my house, I came up to my uncle's house, [redacted] We asked him to join us. He counselled us to flee; however, he said that he didn't want to leave, that he wasn't healthy enough to go, and that he was unwilling to leave his home and that he was staying home no matter what. That is what I know about him. He stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the woods? Was it until your arrest that you already mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I got into the woods on the 1st of May, and up there in the woods, we arranged for a place to sleep behind a rock. There were shells that were still falling, so we were afraid that we would get hit by a shell. So we tried to arrange this place behind a big rock. We used evergreen branches, we put that on the ground, and then we had taken some blankets. In the evening it rained, so we tried to cover ourselves with plastic. My children were still underaged. They had a small tent for two persons. There were lots of us from the village there. We were all together in a group. However, I can't tell you how many people were there exactly. Then we lit a fire, but we didn't want the smoke to be seen. So that's why we did it only during the night. We tried to prepare some food there but --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you. We do not need all these details. My question was, actually: How long did you stay in the woods? Please answer this question and focus on my questions, please.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I stayed in the woods until the 4th of May. That's when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And during these days, was Jelec shelled all the time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: All the time, from two directions, Miljevina and Kalinovik. Every three minutes, three shells. It was shelled all the time. It was being hit all the time. In those days, we would go out to a meadow and watch these shells falling on Jelec. Most of them fell around Relji [phoen], Gradina, the centre of Jelec. You could see explosions and places where shells fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was Jelec taken over by Serb soldiers at a point in time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers did not come to Jelec. They took over Jelec on the 4th of May. They took Jelec over on the 4th of May, when Jelec was attacked from all sides by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they remain, the people, in Jelec, or did the people in woods fight back? Did they ever fight back again these Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know. Let's go back to some of these details. On the 4th of May, we heard shells. Shells were falling. We were there. Sometime around 11.00, a man came to this place where we were and said, "Let's get going from here. The Serb army, the Chetniks, have arrived to the village of Palez. There are ten buses there and they are coming from behind our backs." Then we started fleeing further into the woods, higher up, into the rocky areas. There was panic, there was fear. As we were running uphill, say, 500 metres later, my older daughter was not there. She got lost somewhere. I returned to that place in order to find my daughter. Some people who were passing by were there, and I asked whether they had seen my daughter. They said that she had gone in the direction of Palez. I went in that direction, 300 or 400 metres, and then I came across the Serb soldiers and that's when I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before we continue with what happened to you after you had been taken prisoner, what happened to your uncle? And please do not repeat his name. Just call him your uncle. We know his name now.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: In the meantime, that is to say, in the period between the 1st and the 4th of May, my uncle was at home. His son went every day or every other day and gave him food to eat at home. So he went to see him. He went down surreptitiously, but he was home alive and well. What happened on that day, I don't know. I found out about that only later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you find out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I found out about that at the camp in KP Dom. I was brought to the camp on the 5th of May, and ten days later, I found out from people who were being brought in from town that my uncle had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did your wife confirm this after your release?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: No. Let me add something else. People who were brought in told me that Jelec had been totally burned down, that everything had been burned down and that 35 people were killed in Jelec and among these people was my uncle as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did your wife confirm this later on when you saw her again after your release?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes. My wife spent the night of the 6th of May in the forest. They took us away, and she stayed in the woods with the children and some other women, 10, 12, I don't know how many. The next morning she went down to the village. She came to my uncle's house. She found him dead there in front of the house. He was lying on the ground, and apparently somebody had come before she came. He had a red rag on his face. He was lying on the back. There was a gunshot wound in his chest. This was an exit/entry wound. It went through his back. One of his legs had burned down since the house had burned and he was at the threshold, and then one leg had burned, that side of his trousers, and one sock. So she left him there. She left. She didn't even go to my house because there was smoke coming out of it. She was afraid to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your wife, how was she able to make out what kind of a wound it was your uncle had? What did she do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: She came up to him and she looked. She saw these gunshot wounds in the chest, as she said. These were exit/entry wounds. They had gone through the back. You could see this on the back, how these bullets got out. She was not afraid to turn him and to look. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of profession does your wife have that she dared to turn your uncle around?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: She didn't know that my uncle was dead. She went to see the house, to have a look. She came across him and he was lying there dead. But she was, by profession, a medical technician, a nurse. [redacted] [redacted]. So she took care of a lot of patients during those years. So she wasn't afraid of such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. You said that you were arrested on the 4th of May. Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I told you already. I went through the woods to look for my daughter. I was calling out her name. I was calling it out loud. In the meantime, as I was walking, on the ground five metres away from me there was a line of soldiers lying on the ground. They were lying down a slope, 10 or 15 of them, and then 10 or 15 of them on the other side, and they all pointed their rifles at me and said, "Here comes a scout. Hands up." And I put my hands up. One of them -- one of them held me at gunpoint and walked up to me. I kept my hands up. He searched me from the head downwards. Then he took off my trousers, he took off my boots. He asked me where my grenades were, where my weapons were. I didn't have anything on me. I just had my hunting knife. He took it off and threw it to the side. I put on my trousers. The one who was holding me at gunpoint walked up to me and put his hands round my neck, moved me about three or four metres, pushed me up a tree and said that he would shoot me there. Would you like me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would rather you answer my questions and not to hear all these details. These soldiers, were they Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: These were soldiers who had olive-green/grey uniforms on. They were not camouflage military uniforms. They were olive-green/grey soldiers' uniforms, those that NCOs usually wore. They all wore the same kind of clothes. They were carrying automatic weapons. There were machine-guns, there were also semi-automatic rifles. There was the insignia of the Yugoslav People's Army. It was the military, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I asked you if they were Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Serb soldiers. Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did these soldiers threaten you or insult you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: The one who grabbed me by the neck and who pushed me up that tree, he said also that he would shoot me there. He said to me, "What are you doing here? Why did you come here? To organise an uprising?" And he was cursing my Ustasha mother. He said that he would nail me to that tree. He pointed his rifle to my heart. I could see those yellow bullets in the rifle. I was really terrified then. My legs went numb. I felt my entire body quivering. It went all the way up to my head, and then, all of a sudden, all fear was lost. At that moment, the man who was holding me at gunpoint introduced himself to me. He said, "Do you know me?" I said that I did know him. He introduced himself though. He said that his name was Jasmin Beckovic, the son of Bego Beckovic. He said, "Why are you so terrified? Your daughter is there. We found her with two old women. There's nothing wrong with her." Then the one who was holding me up to the tree let go of me and said, "What's wrong with you? You had a house, you had an apartment, you had a car. You don't like Yugoslavia. You want a sovereign Bosnia, and now I'm going to give Pijesak, the SDA and Alija to you. Where is your commander? How many machine-guns do you have? How many weapons do you have?" I said that we haven't even got a Colonel there, that there is no military, no soldiers, no weapons, no nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you. I would like you to answer my questions and not give that many details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm going to emphasise that, sir. I know that you want to tell us all of this, but we are limited to issues beyond which you are going. We are not here to determine these sorts of matters. What we are very interested in is the evidence which you can give in relation to the matters we do have to determine. So please just answer the questions without going on to tell us everything you know about what happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were other villagers detained on the same day by the same group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: On the same day, another six men were detained with me. I was the seventh. On the same day, we were transported to the KP Dom in Foca, the camp in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you and these other six men were arrested, were women arrested, women and children arrested as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Together with us, I don't know exactly. There was my wife, my children, and many other children, women, and elderly people. We were all transported together beyond the village of Jelec and the hamlet of Zelasi [phoen]. They stayed somewhere behind, and the seven of use taken on. They said they were taking us to the commander to be interrogated. When we arrived at Jelec, there were buses waiting there, and then we were transported to Foca, and we arrived there in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were the women and children separated from the men, at which place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: That was in the village of Laza. In fact, beyond the village of Laza, about 100 metres away, there is the former railway which is now abandoned. There was a crevice there, and we were separated there from the women. They remained up there, and we were taken from the village of Laza to Jelec and onwards from Jelec.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you get to Laza and later on to Jelec? Did you all have to walk from the place of arrest to Laza?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: We walked all the way to the village of Laza, and from then on, we took the so-called upper railway. They drove us down the rails for a couple of hundred metres, the seven of us, and in a spot where there was a deep crevice, they told us to sit down. They were wondering what to do with us. There were 20 or 30 soldiers there. We were wondering what they were going to do with us and they told us they were waiting for Vojo, the commander. Then Vojo came, accompanied by this seventh man. They put him together with us and three machine-guns and rifles were pointed at us. When Vojo arrived -- he had the rank of captain. He had three stars on his sleeve. He climbed down to this hole with us. There were children among us. He said the children are completely innocent. He was looking at a child, and he told us, "What have you done? What do you want a sovereign Bosnia for? Why are you unhappy with Yugoslavia? You have no weapons to fight with." He told us to shut up and to go in front of them. That's how we arrived at Ravna Seoca

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you. Please do not give us all these details. Just answer my questions. On your way on foot to Jelec, did you see Muslim villages burning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: When we passed the village of Seoca, we came to a height, so-called Gajei from which we could see the village of Jelec, Govze, Podgaj, Ratina, Podgaj. Everything was burning, and the houses were already burnt down. We could see crows in the air and other birds. It was eerie. All the houses were burned down by that time. I could see my own house, my old house in flames and many other houses. There was a lot of shooting with submachine-guns and all kinds of weapons, and everything was burnt down: Ratine, Banjine, Gradac and so forth

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: These villages that you just mentioned, are these Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: All of these were Muslim villages. Above the village of Govze, near the woods, there were about ten Serbian houses. They were not on fire and they were never burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were walking and while you saw these burning houses, did you or anyone else in your group refer to the houses? Did a soldier make remarks about the burning houses?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: They didn't say anything, but somewhere by the village of Laza, we climbed down to the first village and a soldier asked me, "Are these Muslim houses?" I said, "Yes, they are." We were walking in front and those houses were being set on fire behind us by the soldiers who were walking behind. However, in front of us, there were also houses on fire, but we didn't come near them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did a woman ask a soldier what she should do now that her house was burning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: That happened before, in the place called Gaj. A woman asked, "Where are you driving us? Where are we going to go now that our houses have burnt down?" A soldier said, "You won't need any where we're taking you."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you saw Jelec burning. Does Jelec have a mosque and was it burning too?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: We didn't see it then from the smoke. We couldn't see what was going on in Jelec, but when we came to the village of Laza and there was a place called have a Vranica or Glavica near Jelec, houses were burning by the road. We couldn't pass through and they told us to sit down. There was shooting from the houses, and they said, "You keep saying you have no weapons, and just look at this shooting from the houses." They were looking for two men, and they said if they didn't find them, they would shoot us. Then we continued on our way. A transmission pole fell, an electricity transmission pole, and blocked the road. We arrived at the place called Glavica, near Jelec. When we arrived there, I could see that the mosque had burnt down and the tower was gone. The carpet factory was burning, the whole centre was burning. I couldn't even see the carpet factory from the smoke. In the meantime these two soldiers who were setting houses on fire were found. They were black with soot. I actually knew these two soldiers. Guns were pointed at us, and they wanted to shoot us straight away, but the soldiers who were escorting us didn't let them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, when you reached Jelec, and you mentioned already the buses that were waiting, where were the buses waiting and what happened at the buses?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: We couldn't pass through the centre of Jelec. We passed by the mosque, by the river of Govze, and we passed by the sawmill. We went across the bridge to the other bank of the river of Govze where the former railway station was. The road widened in that place. There were about 50 military vehicles, some buses, jeeps, and we were driven in front of them along the road. As we came closer to the troops, they were taking off the knives from their rifles. They lined us up, and behind our backs they put the knives in the back of our necks. These soldiers did not -- were not wearing olive-grey, drab uniforms. They were dressed in various clothes. They were dirty. They had long beards. And they started beating people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they even start -- try to kill you or did they intend to kill you? Did they say anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I was on the verge of a breakdown. I could only feel this knife on the skin of my neck. The people who were next to me were being beaten. One soldier was carrying a big photo of Tito and hit a man next to me on the head. He broke his nose. He was saying, "I found this in your house, and there is no more Tito to defend you." But nobody hit me at that moment. Then there was the defence of the village of Jajkovici beyond that railway station. From up there, the troops were carrying something in white sheets. The sheets were covered with blood. I was afraid they might be carrying bodies. I had a feeling they were going to kill us. By the road where we were sitting, there were a lot of goods just thrown on the ground from various shops, wrapped in sheets. But what they were carrying in those sheets were actually calves. They were going to a --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: -- an assembly place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you, and please do not give me all these details. Simply answer my questions. Did you board the buses or did you board vehicles that took you to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Locals from various places came to the assembly place. Soldiers were already on board these buses. As we were getting on, we were beaten. I remember at one point we fell on our knees, and they told us not to look at the soldiers. They beat us then. And as we were to board a bus, one driver said, "I'm not going to take these people in until this stops." So they stopped beating us. Then we boarded the bus, and the bus started towards Miljevina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The bus driver who actually prevented further beating and mistreatment, was he a civilian or was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. He wasn't wearing an uniform. I know that much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From Jelec, where were you taken, straight to the KP Dom or somewhere else first?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: They took us to Miljevina. We stopped in front of a motel in Miljevina. As far as we could see from the back windows, there was a welcome party made up of the locals. They got off the buses. They fired shots into the air. They hugged and kissed with the local people. Then they got on the bus again, and we started towards Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you go in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: On the bus, on our way to Foca, they forced us to sing certain songs. I won't say which. On the intersection at the road near Kopilovo, on wait to Tjentiste, we stopped. There was an awning and a sort of podium near the road. We got off the bus there with our hands behind our heads. There were a lot of soldiers there in parade uniforms and in camouflage uniforms. There was a man there called Cosa, and besides him there was Zoran Vukovic. Cosa ordered us to kiss the Serbian flag which was put up high, and he told us to kiss that flag and to make the sign of the cross, and we failed to do that, they would cut off two of our fingers. Since that was the threat, Cosa told someone to get pliers to make the threat more real. So people from the bus stepped out and kissed the flag, and when it was my turn, I did the same. Then we went to the primary school, which was 20 or 30 metres away from that place, and we entered the staff room of that school.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Boro Ivanovic in the school or near the school?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I saw him in the staff room of that school but not before.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was he? What was his position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I don't know what his position was. In the staff room, we sat on the floor, one or two metres away from each other, and they brought a Serbian soldier into that room, by the name of Majdof. I had worked in Focatrans before. He beat that soldier and slapped him on the face. It was so horrible that we were frighten. He justified himself mentioning some papers. They asked him why he didn't take part in that action in Jelec. He was showing some papers to justify himself and the person who was beating him did not believe him and continued slapping him and beating him. Then he went from one to another of us, and I put my hands on my stomach to protect myself. He kicked me on the face and broke two of my teeth. Then he left that room, and he didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said you did not know what position he had. Did he wear a uniform, a military uniform? I mean Boro Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: He had a military uniform, and what his position was, I don't know. This soldier who was beaten was being punished for failing to report to that unit, which went -- which attacked Jelec. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you, afterwards, were also kicked, and the others as well, the other Muslims present as well. Who did that, Boro Ivanovic or someone else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: No. Boro only kicked each of the seven of us once and slapped us once on the face each, and then he left the room and he didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you beaten by other soldiers as well on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: There were no soldiers. There were three men in camouflage uniforms. I know two of them, and I don't know the third one. There was also a fourth one wearing a police uniform and a beret on his head. That man didn't touch us and didn't beat us, whereas the three others did beat us. They went from one to another, beating us, and the most violent one was Jankovic and another one, Zelenovic, nicknamed Zelja. I don't know the third man. I would recognise him, but I don't know who he is. He was wearing a reserve police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did anyone intervene and stop these beatings at a point in time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: It got a little better after that. Two of our people were taken out for ten minutes, and then they would come back to that room. After that, Radivoje Jegdic came to that room in civilian clothes. He had jeans, some sort of jacket, and a pistol in his belt. When he arrived, all beating stopped. He asked me, "How are you?" We knew each other. He asked after my children. He was very nice and decent. All beating stopped, as I said. Nobody beat us any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you taken to the KP Dom then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Then we were ordered to clean that room and tidy it up. Shall I tell you the details?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. Please tell us where were you taken.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Then we were taken out of that room. Night had fallen already. We were taken outside the building. Above the road there was a wall. We were lined up against that wall, and somebody, behind our backs, said we should all be executed. A soldier came up to me. He put his bayonet, the knife on his rifle, to my neck, and while this was happening, somebody was making a list. He was putting our names -- taking our names down, including my name. He said that we should be executed then and there. But then he changed his mind, and he said, "Take them to the Drina bridge. Kill them and throw them off the bridge." Then he changed his mind again, and he said, "They're not worth the ammunition. Put them on the bus again, take them to Kopilovo, kill them with clubs and throw them into Potocina [phoen]." Until Then I was afraid that they would kill me but I was scared that the club wouldn't hit me the right way and I wouldn't be killed straight away. Then a vehicle came and they put us into that vehicle. Three of us sat in the back. There was a driver, and there was a man sitting across from us. He kept us at gunpoint. He told us to look at the roof of the vehicle. We started towards Kopilovo, but then they made an U-turn, and because I knew the place and knew the road, I understood we were going towards Foca. At some point we arrived at a place that was lit. There was light outside. Then I recognised the KP Dom. We had arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know what time it was? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It might have been 10.00 p.m., maybe 9.00 p.m. It was night, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were all seven of you taken to the KP Dom? On the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, all seven of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the KP Dom until then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I was taken away from the KP Dom on the 8th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, who received you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: We got off that vehicle. We put our hands behind our heads. I recognised, in front of the KP Dom, people who worked there before the war, policemen wearing police uniforms. There were several people in camouflage uniforms. There was one man named Prodanovic in a soldier's olive-grey uniform, and they took us to a room right next to the entrance to the KP Dom. There they searched us. They searched our pockets. I had a comb. I had a handkerchief. I had a watch on my hand. Risto Ivanovic frisked me and then I was also searched by the man in the uniform, Prodanovic. He took away my comb and my handkerchief and he left my watch. Then they took us inside the KP Dom. Risto took us through the compound, through the yard, and we were taken to the building on the right-hand side. We climbed three stone steps. We went upstairs and were taken to a room where Risto left us. The rooms were empty. There was no write there. We could see only the street lights outside. He left us in that room. He said, "You have no blankets. You have nothing. You just have a carpet here," and he showed a carpet in the hall and he said, "Try to use this as a blanket."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I like to show the witness the photograph Exhibit 18, photograph 7512.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you please show us in which room you were taken? You have to show us on the ELMO, not on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I came this way. I climbed the stairs, and I came to this room here. These two windows overlook the yard. Those windows belong to another room, and I was in this room. That was Room 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness has just pointed out the floor above the ground floor in the building number 2. We refer to this room actually as Room 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right. That is Room 18 that he's pointing to, the one on the corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's enough. And I think it's time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did he come in a group of detainees from Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: You mean the camp of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. When he came to the KP Dom, was he in a group of villagers from Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes. He was in a group of 47 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, before the war and during your confinement, did you suffer from a heart condition?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes. I had angina pectoris.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you get treatment and the necessary medication for your heart condition while you were detained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I did not get any medication. After I came to the camp, 10 or 15 days later - I don't know exactly - Gojko, the male nurse from the prison -- no, not Gojko. Well, a guard came and said, "Who has a problem can go to see a doctor." Several of us in the room reported sick, but he chose only three, and I was one of the three to go to see the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually see a doctor, or did you see this nurse that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: We were taken to that building number 1. That was on the second or third floor, I don't know exactly. We were taken by guards. Gojko received us there. I was seen by Dr. Cedo Dragovic. He examined me. He didn't really examine me because I was blue in the face. He didn't even ask me what was wrong or, rather, he did ask me what was wrong. I said I had pain in the chest. He prescribed some kind of medicine for me. He sent me to another room telling me that Gojko should give it to me. When I came to Gojko's, that medicine wasn't there. Then I returned to his room again, although I was not supposed to do that. I did that at my own initiative. Drago, the doctor, received me again. He got up from his chair, and he took from his cupboard a cream that was manufactured by Galenika from Belgrade, and it was a cream that sportsmen were supposed to use when they would get injured in any way, so then -- it was also supposed to be used for massage. So that's what I took.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever get medication for your angina pectoris?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I never got medicine for my angina pectoris. In the meantime, people who were with Gojko when lice appeared, people from my room, that is, Gojko went with people from my room to spray something round the beds, and then from that man I got two or three tablets. I asked for nitroglycerine. I got Trinidil, something like that. That was the name. I don't know whether I'm pronouncing it right. So I got three or two Trinadils, and I used them from time to time. That's the only medicine I got for angina pectoris.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the person with the name Ibrahim Sandal in your room, or do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I know that person. He came after me, I think in the month of May. He was put up in a room opposite mine on the left-hand side. That's where he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you mean a room in the set of rooms where you were in so that you could see him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: He was on the same floor. I just had to cross through the anteroom of my room to get to his room. On that floor there were four rooms with a big anteroom between these four rooms. So I would go to his room, and he would come to my room. He was so sick. I did not know him. He was brought from the village of Kunovo. He was sick. He was lying on a blanket on the floor behind the door, and he was all blue from his eyes to the waist. He was all black and blue when he undressed to show me. He told me that he could hardly breathe, that he couldn't turn as he lay there. So I used the cream I got, and then I put that cream on his chest and on his back a few times. He said that that did him well, and he thanked me for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did Mr. Sandal get treatment for his sickness?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about that. I can't say. I can't say whether he was taken somewhere, treated somewhere. I don't know about that. Most probably not. Nobody went for treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he ever recover?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: While I was there, he was in my room. He was very nervous. After that, he got all yellow. He was all yellow in the face and in the body. He could hardly breathe. He would choke as he was breathing. We would see him smoking as we were coming back from lunch. He would take grass, pluck grass and clover, and he'd smoke this grass and clover. That's not a good thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you. My question was: Did he ever recover while you were there? You hadn't answered that.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: No, he did not recover. I think that he was one of the more serious patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has just described -- Ibrahim Sandal in 5.25 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were Serb prisoners detained in the KP Dom, and if so, where were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: In the KP Dom, there were Serb detainees as well. They kept them opposite our building on the left. They were on the second or the third floor. I don't know. There were some former convicts from the KP Dom, and there were also some Serb detainees in camouflage uniforms, in olive-green/grey uniforms, in civilian uniforms. I don't know how many there were. There were always ten, 15, or 20. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you meet or see them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: They were moving around the compound as we were in our rooms. They were playing soccer in the compound. They were moving about. They were going out for lunch. We could hear the television and radio in our room. We heard the sounds from their room. Also, we could hear Serb news, the musical instrument called gusle on television and also, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we do not have to talk about the living conditions because we have heard that evidence already from other witnesses. I just want to know something very particular. When did you have opportunity to shower or to wash properly while you were detained, for the first time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I think it was July, the end of July or the beginning of August. I don't know exactly. Until then, we hadn't taken any baths or we hadn't shaved. We didn't have any soap. We had grown big beards. We were dirty. We were awful. In the meantime, guards came and told us to clean our rooms, to sweep them clean. At that moment, a barber came, too. This barber was from Foca. His name was Halim Dedovic. Then he started giving us all haircuts. Then he ordered us to put soap on our faces by ourselves, and then he would shave us, too. Then we went to take baths in groups for the very first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what happened afterwards? Did you see journalists afterwards, after that had happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: A day or two or three days later, in the compound one morning we saw the warden of the camp together with four or five people, civilians. They wore blue suits. I think there were two women there. They crossed the compound, went to the carpentry shop toward the compound, and then in building number 1, in the yard, as you enter that building, they put up a camera. They took pictures of that building there. On that building, the convicts showed up at the windows looking through bars. They offered them cigarettes. This woman did. They tried to take pictures of that. In the meantime, Rasevic -- there was a girl from the hospital there who was an interpreter. She had long hair. I don't know her name. She spoke English. We watched this on the sly from our rooms, and then Rasevic said that these cameramen could take pictures no longer. He took them away, and he did not allow them to do that kind of work any more. He did not allow any filming, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said the warden was with these people. What was he wearing; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: The warden wore an olive-green/grey military uniform, and on the left side of his belt he carried a gun. That's how he was dressed. A pistol. Actually, on the right-hand side he wore a pistol, I remember that well. Olive-green/grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We will come to the warden later in your testimony. Just another question related to the living conditions. Did the living conditions, especially the lack of food, affect your health?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: The living conditions were difficult. Food was poor. There was very little food, exceptionally little. The hygienic conditions were hard. If there was water, there wasn't soap. It was even difficult to go to the toilet. There wasn't anything that we could wash and bathe with and shave with. The conditions were horrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not asking you about the conditions. As I said, we have already heard this evidence. Did they affect your physical health? If so, what did you suffer?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I had pain from the blows I had sustained at Brod. I had pain in my back and in my ribcage. When I would lie down, it would be difficult for me to get up. That really troubled me. I had trouble with my angina pectoris. I weighed 95 kilogrammes when I came to the camp, and I got out with 54 kilogrammes. I was supposed to lose weight because of my angina pectoris. I had lost a lot of weight, so perhaps it was easier for me to bear the angina pectoris since I had lost all that weight, although I did have crises. My right shoulder, my right arm, would go numb. When I had these crises, this Trinidil that I got, those two or three tablets, were of crucial importance at these moments. I would lie still, I would take this Trinidil, and that's how it would pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you interrogated while you were detained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I don't know the exact date. I think it was June or July. I cannot confirm that. I was not interrogated soon after my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arrival, but I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: One day, one morning as I was in my room, number 18, a guard named Dobriljo Pljevaljcic came. He called out my name, read it out from a little piece of paper, and also read out the name of a certain Dedovic. I forgot his first name. He was walking in front of me. I walked behind him, and then he escorted us to the gate, and from the gate he told us to go to the right, to walk upstairs. We walked up a flight of stairs in the administration building of the KP Dom. I stood in front of one office and the other one stood in front of the other office, and that's where we waited for our interrogation. It was in that office that I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on your way to the interrogation room, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Nobody beat me until I got to the very entrance from the external side of the KP Dom. There were two or three civilians there. Among these civilians was an acquaintance of mine who set out towards me. He was proffering his hand. He wanted to shake hands. Then Dobriljo hit me with his rifle in the back, and he said, "To the left." And that's the only thing I managed to say to this man. I said, "Hello," and then I was hit very badly, and then I went upstairs. Nobody beat me after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The three civilians that you just mentioned, you mean detainees or who were they?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: They were civilians from town. If necessary, I can mention the name of that person. I know this one man but I don't know the other two.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what is the name of this man?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: That man was a colleague of mine from the school. His name was Vide Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he doing there? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: He was a teacher at the school centre. He had the same kind of job as I did. He was involved in vocational training.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he doing there? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: You mean there at the KP Dom when I saw him?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: I don't know. I never saw him again. I never saw him at the KP Dom after that. And what he was doing there then, I really don't know. It was just a moment. He saw me, and he just proffered his hand because he wanted to shake hands with me, nothing else. That's all. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: We waited a bit and then I got into the room. Paprica interrogated me. I can't remember his first name. I used to know his first name. And there was also Vojo Starovic and yet another man who was sitting in a chair. He wore a leather jacket. Later on, I found out that that was the deputy warden of the camp. His name was Gagovic. Also, there was Mico Rasevic, Mitar Rasevic, there from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Paprica, who was he? What kind of function did he have? Was he a policeman or a military person?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: He wore a police uniform, the kind they wore before the KP Dom. And Vojo had the same kind. However, the one who was sitting at the chair had a yellow jacket, and he kept staring at me. I didn't know who that was, but later on I found out that was Gagovic. I don't know his first name. Whereas Rasevic had a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Starovic, what did he wear, and who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Vojo Starovic? I know the man. He used to work at the school centre before he had a degree in economics. He worked after that in Maglic as an economist. He had a police uniform. He was an interrogator

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this person Gagovic that the witness just mentioned is listed in P-3, on the list of employees, under number 79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What were you asked during the interrogation? What was it focused on?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Paprica was sitting at the desk. Vojo was walking about. Gagovic was just sitting there. He didn't ask me anything. Mr. Vojo was quite fair to me. He asked me how I was, where my children were, where my wife was. He offered me a cigarette. He treated me fairly. It was very hard for me. Paprica took a big yellow piece of paper in front of the drawer. He put it in front of himself. First he looked for me there, and then apparently he asked me about all my details, my name, surname, whether I did any military service, whether I had any children, what I was doing, where I worked, things like that, and then he looked at this yellow piece of paper again. These were some kind of notes. He asked me where I was engaged in Foca. He said that when my apartment was searched in the [redacted], he said they found a box where a machine-gun had been in my apartment, and also they found that kind of rope that was used for cleaning machine-guns. And also I was in the company of Salko Borcak. That's what he said to me. I said to him that I knew Salko Borcak only by sight, that I was never in that company, that I did not have a machine-gun, that I did not have this thing to clean rifles with. But then I did have a box where a machine-gun would be stored, because I bought that at a dump in Sarajevo many years before that. That's where I kept my very own pistol. That's where I kept it locked, because I was afraid that my children might touch it and that there could be an accident.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you threatened during the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: At that moment, nobody threatened me, none of them, that is. Then they continued to interrogate me. They were asking me why I had gone to my village of Jelec, why was I there, why was I not in Foca, how was I captured there. They asked me about all of that, how that happened, who captured me, do I know these people, who are these people, who took my pistol up there, where is my pistol. That's what the interrogation was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the interrogators draft a written statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: They wrote an entire sheet of paper, and then on the other page they almost filled out that one too. And Then Paprica was typing this at the typewriter, at the desk. When Paprica finished this, he said to me: "This statement of yours is no good. You haven't said a thing. This has been written in five or six copies, and you are going to sign this statement for me. This statement of yours is no good. One copy will go to the Crisis Staff, another one will go to some other place." I have no idea. I can't remember where all these copies were supposed to be sent to. "Now, what the Crisis Staff says will remain to be seen. This is not good. If the Crisis Staff returns you for another interrogation, you will be beaten pretty badly." Do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What else did he tell you, yes, in relation to your statement and the Crisis Staff, if anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Then he said to me, "In the Crisis Staff, there is your Cedo Zelovic, Vojo Maksimovic ..." And he said "your Cedo Zelovic" because we were friends. We were great friends. We were colleagues. We held each other in high regard. We were close. He said, "In the Crisis Staff is your Cedo Zelovic, then also Vojo Maksimovic, Ostojic, Cancar, Radovan Mandic, Miro, Miro Stanic, and the warden of the KP Dom." They told me that there were seven people there. I don't know whether I mentioned all of them. And he said, "If the Crisis Staff returns this, things will not go well for you." At that moment, Vojo said, "I know this man." Oh, yes. They asked me whether I was a member of the Party of Democratic Action. I said that I was not a member of that party, of any party. Vojo said, "I know this man. This man was only engaged in his own work," things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these people that you just listed and that you said that they were, according to Paprica, in the Crisis Staff, did you know these people, all of them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: The people he enumerated, yes, I knew them all personally, all of them. I knew them well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were they politicians in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-69
utterances.text: Politicians from Foca were Vojo Maksimovic, Ostojic, whose first name I forget. Petko Cancar was a politician. Radovan Mandic was a doctor in a hospital.
